Exactly like that, yes--that's where I got the idea, in fact. I have a couple of those little cast iron pans, but I usually make a full-size cake and then just cut pieces to serve with ice cream.

And goodness, I wouldn't want anyone to get hurt. :-) It's a basic Nestle Tollhouse/Arm & Hammer cookie recipe, but (IMO) it's the butterscotch chips that make all the difference; they really add to the buttery cookie flavor.

So:

Preheat oven to 350F--or if you're using a dark nonstick pan, 325F--it really doesn't matter that much, but it is better to use the lower temp for a dark nonstick pan; if you're going to err in cooking these, you want to err on the side of slightly less done instead of overdone. Prep a basic 13 x 9 cake pan--I have one of those brownie pans with the grid insert, but any cake pan is fine--by spreading a little butter on it and placing parchment on top of the butter. You really need the parchment for this because you're going to take the cookies out of the pan while they're still gooey/sticky. (Tip: most butter wrappers end up with juuust enough butter still sticking to them to grease a pan. I save all my butter wrappers in a drawer in the fridge for just this purpose.)

1 C butter--unsalted if you have it, but you can use salted and then just cut a little of the salt later or have a little more saltiness in the cookie; there's not enough salt in the recipe to make the cookie salty, and I like a little salt in my sweets anyway, so it's entirely up to you.

**3/4 C white sugar

3/4 C light brown sugar**

Beat those together in a mixing bowl until light/fluffy/well combined. Scrape the sides so you don't end up with a layer of plain butter stuck to it that needs to be combined by hand later. (I just tilt the bowl of my stand mixer to do this--I have a paddle with a silicone scraper edge, so I don't need to stop the mixer to scrape.)

Now add:

2 eggs, beating in one at a time

2 tsp/1 T vanilla--I actually just slosh it in, but it's around that amount. That's more vanilla than the recipe calls for but I like more vanilla in there. Sometimes I add a little butter flavor/extract, too, if I'm using cheaper (and therefore less flavorful) butter; Kerrygold is my preference, but it's pricey here, sigh, so I often end up just using the Walmart brand unsalted butter, which is fine--it's actually a pretty decent-quality butter, not overly watery like many cheap butters--but not very flavorful.

Beat until combined.

In a separate bowl (you can just throw these in one at a time, but I usually give them a stir in a separate bowl and then add them in together), stir together:

2 1/4 C plain/AP flour

1 tsp salt (if using salted butter, I make this a scant tsp)

1 tsp baking soda

Mix that into the wet ingredients in two batches--you just throw it all in, but adding all the dry ingredients at once to my stand mixer means some of it flies over the top when the mixer starts moving.

When that's combined, add:

1 C semisweet chocolate chips

**1 C butterscotch chips

1/2 C dark chocolate chips

1/2 C caramel chips** (Hershey's and Godiva both make these; I usually use the Godiva because the Hersheys are hard to find, but I actually prefer the Hersheys, which smell like a delicious caramel-y dream. The Godiva ones are kind of big and don't smell as good--still good, but not as good. I usually put the dark chocolate chips and caramel chips in one cup, like I fill it a little under halfway with the dark chocolate and then top it off with caramel.)

Spread the dough in the pan--it doesn't have to be perfectly flat or anything, but try to get it fairly even; I generally make sure the center is a little lower, a slight valley in the middle, to help it bake evenly--and place it in the 350F (or 325F) oven for twelve minutes. At the twelve-minute mark, turn the pan around and set the timer for another 12 minutes (depending on your oven, of course, but generally it'll bake for 20-25 minutes).

I take the ice cream out of the freezer at the twelve-minute-mark when I turn the pan, so it has time to soften a little before serving--I like it to really melt into the cookie, so I want to facilitate the melting. (Oh, and I just use plain vanilla for this, which I think most places do; you could use chocolate, I imagine, but I think vanilla is the flavor you really want here. Caramel ice cream might be nice, too, if you want to try a different flavor.)

When the cake is done--it will be golden brown and puffy, basically, and a toothpick inserted in the middle will come out dry or with a few damp crumbs stuck to it. It's hard to test one of these because often the pick will come out covered with chocolate, so I don't always bother; if your oven gets even close to the right temperature, 24 minutes is plenty--take it out of the oven. Have your bowls or whatever ready, and immediately cut pieces of whatever size you want--you'll need a spatula or something to get them out of the pan, the cake is too hot for even me to lift out with my fingers--and place them in the bowls, and immediately top with however much ice cream you want. For me it's generally about a half scoop or a single scoop--I often just use a big spoon instead of a scoop, so it's not a perfect little round ball on there, but it's about that much. Again, for me the goal is not ice cream and cookie, the goal is cookie soaked in melted ice cream to make a warm gooey slurry of sorts, so...personal taste, really.

I have this "Torani" brand caramel sauce, which is meant to go on top of whipped cream on coffee and is delicious, that I sometimes put on top of the ice cream, to add even more of that lovely buttery caramel-y flavor, but that's optional. Or you can use chocolate sauce or butterscotch sauce or whatever you want, or you can leave it off if you want, too. It adds a nice layer of flavor but it's certainly not necessary.

...and that's it, really. Unfortunately, you can't really "re-bake" the cookie to do this again, though you could certainly try microwaving it--I don't own a microwave, so I've never tried it, but I would think any textural loss/toughness caused by the microwave would be covered up by the ice cream's moisture. For us, this is a Friday night dessert and then we just have the cookie cake as normal through the rest of the week, because it's really good all on its own.

For me, it's the butterscotch chips that make the difference. I tried adding them on a whim about a year ago and have never made a cookie cake without them since; they add a really nice extra flavor to it. I mean, really, the plain cake part of a chocolate chip cookie is basically a butterscotch flavor anyway--butter, vanilla, and brown sugar (though butterscotch is usually made with dark brown sugar, and I think dark brown sugar is too much for this cookie cake)--so why not intensify that flavor if you can? I've also tried adding toffee chips in the past, and those had a nice flavor, too, and added a nice little crunch, but IMO the butterscotch chips are better (and they smell amazing). Then the dark chocolate chips are there to balance out the added sweetness of the butterscotch chips a little and give the flavor a little more complexity (but I don't want it to be too dark, which is why I only use half a cup of them; just enough to get one every couple of bites). Obviously, you can use whatever chips you like--you can do all dark chocolate, or no dark chocolate, or leave out the caramel, or whatever; I like this combination best, but they're all good.

I get all the ingredients together ahead of time, which is why I have a separate bowl for the dry ingredients and one for the chips, and then I break the eggs into a little bowl; sometimes I add the chips to the flour mix and add all of that at once, too. You can certainly break the eggs directly into the butter/sugar or add the dry ingredients separately or whatever. Like I said I can generally put this together in about ten minutes, so for me the separate bowls make it all go faster: I give the dry ingredients a quick stir in a bowl, the butter and sugars go directly into the bowl of the mixer and I turn that on while I break the eggs, then I pour those in, slosh in the vanilla (and butter extract if I'm using it), wait thirty seconds or so for that to be all combined (I tilt the bowl of the stand mixer to scrape the sides) and then start adding in the dry mix, so the whole mixing process only takes two or three minutes. And the chips only require a few seconds of mixing, just enough to get them evenly throughout the dough.

Last week I forgot the baking soda, lol. The cake still tasted okay, but not quite the same; it didn't color as it baked and the texture wasn't as nice. It was edible, though--the ice cream covers a multitude of sins, heh. (I still threw it out and made a proper one the next day; why eat a substandard cookie if you don't have to? Especially when you're only having one like a normal person, and it's a treat, instead of being your lunch.) If you don't have baking soda, you can use 1/2 tsp or so of baking powder instead; the cake will be more "cakey," but it's better than nothing.

So, yeah, there you go. It's a fantastic cookie cake all on its own--I get requests to make it for friends all the time, and my girls have always been big fans of cookie cake so it's been a staple in our house for over a decade, though I just started using the butterscotch and caramel chips in the last year or so--but piping hot out of the oven with ice cream on top is a whole 'nother level, heh. I'm actually glad you can't re-bake the cookie because I would be tempted to do it every night, lol, and I don't need the calories--but Friday night is kind of our Fun Family Night so I like doing something a little special, and this is so easy and good.

Of course, let me know if you have any questions or anything!
